title: I'm Not Good at the Workplace Politics
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece reframes workplace politics as unavoidable rather than something to opt out of. It separates negative political behavior, such as taking credit for others' work or withholding information, from positive political behavior, such as building strategic relationships and promoting one's contributions honestly. The author argues that ignoring office politics is like trying to avoid raindrops in a storm, and that the real skill is becoming politically intelligent: leveraging influence and relationships ethically rather than through manipulation. The piece closes by urging readers to stay above the negative fray while still engaging constructively with the political reality of organizational life.
points: Negative workplace politics include taking credit for others' work, badmouthing colleagues, and withholding information.
Trying to avoid office politics entirely is compared to avoiding raindrops in a cloudburst, it can't be done.
Positive political behavior, like building relationships that help you get things done, is distinguished from manipulation.
The goal is political intelligence: understanding the intersection of influence and relationships rather than pretending politics don't exist.
Staying above negative politics means not fueling gossip or cliques while still promoting your work and influencing others ethically.
quotes: When others use their authority, influence, and status for personal self-interest, they are operating politically.
This is akin to avoiding raindrops in a cloudburst. Office politics are everywhere. You can’t sit them out.
Becoming politically intelligent is about understanding the intersection of influence and relationships.
Promoting your good work, or leveraging the influence of others, is a world apart from getting ahead through manipulation and putting others down.
Capable colleagues don’t put people down. They lift them up.
